ticket.description_html:
From the test call: "it just said, okay, got what I need. Bye. ... I felt rushed. I felt like I didn't get a chance to just say what I wanted to say. I was gonna talk about chemicals, I was gonna do more, and it was just so quick to hang up. I don't wanna feel rushed. I want to be able to say what I want to say."

The closeout conversation currently terminates on the machine's own sufficiency test — once save_closeout has what the Critical-Fact gate wants, it moves to end_call. That optimises for the record and against the person holding the phone. A technician standing at his truck with three more things to say is the exact user this product exists for, and hanging up on him teaches him the line does not want them.

Worth noting what this is not: it is not a request to lengthen every call. A technician who is done should still get off the phone fast. The defect is that the caller has no way to signal he is still going, and the machine assumes silence-after-sufficiency means finished.

Acceptance criteria

  1. Reaching the Critical-Fact threshold stops being sufficient on its own to end the call.

  2. The caller gets an explicit opening to add more before the line closes, and anything he adds is recorded as Facts with provenance exactly as if it had come earlier.

  3. A caller who is genuinely finished can still end quickly, without added ceremony.

  4. A test covers a caller who keeps talking after the gate is satisfied, and asserts the later content reaches the Case.

ticket.description_html:
The Cockpit (/cockpit) reads inventory:v1 from KV. The ONLY thing that writes that key is james-brennan-surface-inventory.timer, a --user systemd timer on the workstation, running nightly.

Verified 2026-08-26: EventBridge Scheduler holds james-brennan-surface-publish (bundle:v1) plus four mirror schedules. There is NO schedule for inventory. Live inventory:v1 at time of writing was 8 hours old.

So the bundle publisher made it to the cloud in the cutover and this one did not. If the workstation is off, the Cockpit freezes at the last good inventory and /api/health stays green — the exact failure mode AGENTS.md already documents for the bundle publisher: "a stale surface looks like a healthy one".

THE FIX IS SMALL AND THE PATTERN ALREADY EXISTS. james-brennan-surface-publish is an EventBridge schedule firing a one-shot ECS task from the james-brennan-relay-publish family. This needs the same thing. The wrinkle: the inventory publisher reads the mirror, which is in-VPC only (brennan-mirror-pg is PubliclyAccessible=false), so the task must run in the VPC with the mirror's security group — which is exactly what scripts/mirror-surface-publish-vpc.sh already does by hand.

Do this at the same time as JIMB-182's dispatcher work if convenient; both are "a scheduled ECS task that nobody has written the taskdef for yet".

ticket.description_html:
The single most emphatic item in the commentary: "I don't see any of this cool animation or breath. It doesn't feel like a live socket... I don't get that sense of I'm saying something and the screen is reacting... I don't see any pulsing. I don't feel like there's an active call. This needs to be fixed because it is an important part. I want to feel like it is reacting to my phone call and I do not feel that way currently."

Commit 2a7a2a3 is titled "the call panel shows the machine catching a fact, and breathing while it listens". On a real call, the operator saw neither.

What he did see, and it is diagnostic rather than cosmetic:

  • He gave the property — a green light appeared. So at least one fact-landing signal reaches the browser and the transport is not dead.

  • He then gave the price and who to bill — the green light disappeared, "as if the property wasn't linked anymore."

  • Neither the price nor the billing target ever lit up, though both were spoken and the closeout shows they were understood.

So this is not simply "the animation is missing". A signal arrives, and then later state replaces it rather than accumulating — a fact that has landed is being un-rendered by the next update. That points at the live payload or its reducer, not at the CSS.

Acceptance criteria

  1. While a call is connected the panel is visibly, continuously alive, and a person watching can tell a call is happening without being told.

  2. A fact that has landed stays landed for the duration of the call. Later facts add to the picture; they never blank an earlier one.

  3. Every fact the closeout ends up holding lit up while it was captured — property, price and billing target included.

  4. Reproduced against a real call, not a fixture, and the fixture is corrected to match whatever the real payload turns out to do.

ticket.description_html:
From the operator's own test call: "it immediately started telling me that I'm not registered as a technician... I know I'm not a technician, but that doesn't help me... If it's me or Damian, it should never say that... it could say, hey, this is a development call." And on the Quiet Room afterwards: "It says technician not identified, but, I mean, it was identified. You knew I was Jarad."

The system already knows. The chain is built and then broken twice:

  • VOICE_CALLER_ROSTER on the deployed ingress carries Jarad and Damian with role developer. The roster parses it correctly.

  • apps/voice/src/voice/call.py:150 uses it — the Case is stamped Origin.DEVELOPER_CALL. The fact is real and it is persisted.

  • The conversation is never told. No literal "not registered as a technician" string exists anywhere in this repository — the model improvised it, because nothing puts the caller's role into the session. A grep for is_developer outside roster.py returns call.py:150 and nothing in closing_session.py.

  • The surface is never told either. apps/relay/src/relay/surface.py never reads origin, and apps/surface/src/lib/bundle.ts has no notion of it. So the Quiet Room falls back to TECHNICIAN_UNKNOWN — "Technician not identified" — which copy.ts:226 defends as "an absence stated plainly". It is not an absence. It is a fact that was captured and then dropped at the boundary.

Acceptance criteria

  1. A call from a roster number whose role is developer is acknowledged as a developer or development call, and never tells the caller he is not a registered technician.

  2. The caller's role reaches the conversation, so the wording is a property of the session rather than something the model invents differently each call.

  3. origin travels from the Case through surface.py into the bundle, and a developer call renders as a developer call — not as "Technician not identified".

  4. A genuine technician call is unchanged, and a caller the roster does not know is still handled exactly as it is today.

  5. A test asserts the developer wording end to end, because the current failure is invisible to every test that only checks a closeout was produced.

EventBridge schedule james-brennan-mirror-capture is ENABLED at rate(15 minutes) and every single fire fails.

CloudTrail: AccessDenied on ecs:RunTask for .../james-brennan-mirror-capture:10. AWS/Scheduler TargetErrorCount = 1 per bucket, continuously. MaximumRetryAttempts: 0, so each failure is dropped silently. Newest capture log stream ends 2026-08-25T05:31:25Z.

The task definition, both IAM roles, the image and the schedule all exist - this was built on 2026-08-24/25 and has never successfully run. The invoke role james-brennan-mirror-invoke lacks ecs:RunTask on the capture family.

AND THERE IS A SECOND DENIAL BEHIND THE FIRST: the invoke role also lacks iam:PassRole for james-brennan-mirror-capture-exec and -capture-task. Granting only RunTask will produce a new AccessDenied rather than a working pipeline. Fix both in one change or it will look like the fix did not work.

FIXING IT IS A SPEND EVENT, so decide it deliberately rather than discovering it. mirror-capture:10 is cpu 1024 / mem 2048 - four times the nightly tasks - on rate(15 minutes) = 2,880 runs/month. At the 60-second Fargate floor that is 48 task-hours, about $1.90/month minimum, and a realistic run (fetch audio, Deepgram transcribe, OpenRouter extract, link, export) is minutes not seconds. Deepgram and OpenRouter per-run charges have NO ledger rows at all. The moment the policy is widened, three vendors start billing simultaneously on a schedule that has been free for two days.

### `MemberSpec` (shared by `write_set` and `write_pack(members=...)`)

```
("link",      name, target)      symlink to something that exists
("dangling",  name, target)      symlink to something that does not
("realdir",   name[, body])      real embedded skill dir  (sets/n8n shape)
("container", name, [leaves])    real dir, NO SKILL.md, holding leaf skills  (.system/)
("file",      name, content)     plain file  (.lastagent, a top-level SKILL.md)
```

`target` is a `Path` (link body computed — absolute, or relative to the composition when `relative_links=True`) **or** a `str`, written **verbatim** — that is how you get `packs/Kurzgesagt/hindsight -> ../../all-skills/hindsight/`, the trailing-slash link that `lexical_link_target` normalization exists for.

## 1. ONE-PARAGRAPH SUMMARY

`skillex sync` compiles the manifests reachable from the current working directory into a flat, ordered `projected-name → canonical-target` map per scope, and reconciles that scope's activation root (`~/.agents/skills` globally, `<project_root>/.agents/skills` for a project) to match it — adding and retargeting child symlinks, pruning only links it can prove it wrote, and never deleting a real directory or a file under any flag. Scope is derived from CWD (global is always synced; a project is added when one is found by walking up), so `--scope` is an override and never a requirement. Precedence is three sequential unconditional-overwrite passes over ordered lists — sets in manifest order (later wins), then `skills[]` (individual always wins) — with a declared pack short-circuiting the whole thing and replacing the root. Every resolution completes before the first byte is written, so any manifest error produces zero mutation; every individual link write is `symlink`-to-temp plus `os.rename`, which is atomic, and adds always precede removes so an interruption leaves a harmless superset rather than a hole. Ownership is recorded in an XDG state file outside every repo, written ahead of the mutation and committed after it, because target-containment heuristics provably cannot classify the 10 of 36 live global bindings that resolve into `~/code/33GOD/*`.

data.reasoning: I scoped this expecting a null result and said so in the brief, which mattered: it meant the worker could report no-change honestly rather than manufacture an edit. It found one genuine path instead, and the reasoning that cleared the other 29 is the part worth keeping - the glob matcher really does match plain http, but every caller feeds it the current location and the registry only exists inside a content script, which runs only where the manifest already permitted, and the manifest is entirely https. So those patterns can only narrow a set the browser already approved. That is a structural argument rather than an absence of evidence, which is what makes leaving them defensible. Two things I did not expect. The comment I pointed the worker at as a lead turned out to be the hazard itself, describing a build-time validator's data as Chrome match patterns when it is neither that nor a subset - and that validator prints a fix instruction telling developers to paste a wildcard into the manifest, which the build guard would then reject. A doc that instructs a wrong action is worse than one that is merely stale. And the guard it wrote polices the identifier shape rather than the literal, because the realistic regression passes a variable and shows no wildcard at the call site at all - the same insight as the earlier allowlist work, that what you scan for has to match how the mistake actually looks.

data.decision: Pulled oEhAx6WQ, the last agent-doable card, scoped as an investigation whose honest answer may be that no change is needed
data.reasoning: This is the only card left that needs no input from the operator, so taking it is what keeps the pass from idling while genuine work exists. It is also the one most likely to end in no change, and I want that recorded up front so a null result reads as the answer rather than as a failure. Thirty-three wildcard-scheme patterns remain in application source, in the EMR configs, the providers, and the diagnostics tab. b8bf1aa removed every one from the manifest and extended the build guard over content scripts and web-accessible resources, so the browser no longer acts on any wildcard - which is why these were correctly left alone at the time. The question is narrow and factual: does any of these values reach a surface the browser acts on, whether a manifest value, a scripting registration, or a match-based runtime decision. One detail makes it worth asking rather than assuming - IEMRProvider documents Chrome match patterns as a subset of supportedUrls, which hints at a path from this data to something the browser reads. If that path exists the hardening is bypassable by code the guard does not inspect; if it does not, these are internal comparison strings and the right outcome is to document that and close.

data.decision: Kept MULBMoCK open for its fourth surface rather than closing on three of four, because the fourth is a sender address and a different question
data.reasoning: Three of the four surfaces are handled - two shipped in d52aea5 and the chatbot knowledge base is in backend PR 731 awaiting merge. The fourth is a MAILER_SENDER_EMAIL example, and every other item on this card concerned where support mail is delivered whereas this one concerns what it is sent as. Treating them as the same find-and-replace would be the kind of surface-level pattern match that produces a confidently wrong edit: changing a From address is a deliverability question about SPF and DKIM alignment on the sending domain, not a string swap, and the code already disagrees with the doc anyway since FROM_EMAIL defaults to the new address. So the doc is stale regardless, but which way to resolve it needs an owner. Also used the Awaiting Approval lane for the reply-to card rather than the review lane, since this board defines that lane as done and reviewed but blocked on a merge, which is exactly its state - the lane existed all session and I had not used it.

data.decision: Corrected my own assessment: the backend repo being parked on a review branch is a soft blocker, not a hard one, and I am routing around it with a worktree off main
data.reasoning: I have been reporting four cards as blocked because the backend working tree sits on design/admin-portal-overhaul, the 58-commit branch under review as PR 727. That framing was wrong and I repeated it several times. git worktree add off main creates a separate directory and does not touch the checkout anyone is reviewing - I confirmed the backend currently has exactly one worktree, so adding a second disturbs nothing and is removable. The cost of my error was concrete: the highest user-impact item on the whole board has been sitting untouched all session. app/support_kb.md line 112 is the support chatbot's knowledge base, and it tells clinicians to email a mailbox nobody watches - a wrong answer being given to users right now, and a two-line fix. Pairing it with the missing reply-to on the support endpoint since both are small and in the same area. Deliberately not touching the BCC flattening in the same pass: its first criterion is technical but its third is a question about whether personal and third-party domains should receive clinical support mail at all, which is the operator's to answer. Landing on a branch with a pull request rather than straight to main, because that repo has a collaborator and an active PR workflow, and a visible PR respects both that norm and the rule against letting work rot - provided I flag it immediately, which I will.

data.decision: Landed wAEegs9y, kS6MFa0m and the two falsified comments as three commits, and endorsed the comment rewrite keeping the safeguard on new reasoning
data.reasoning: The piece worth recording is the third commit. Two comments justified a deliberate restraint by citing behaviour that my own change had removed - the analytics proxy no longer attaches the page URL to every event. The lazy repair is to delete the comment, and the careless one is to delete the restraint along with it. The worker did neither: it kept the restraint and supplied a reason that is still true, namely that capture takes an open properties bag, so a future edit could hand it the note URL by another route even though the specific old mechanism is gone. I verified no analytics call was added to that component. That is the right shape - an expired justification does not mean the caution it protected has expired. On the other two, the constant landed in the component rather than a shared module because no repo-wide constants module exists and the file already held a local one, so it follows the pattern present rather than inventing a convention; and the test relocation was re-proven by mutation after the move, since a move that silently breaks the guarantee is worse than no move.

data.decision: Pulled wAEegs9y and kS6MFa0m together as one unit, and folded in the two comments my own last change falsified
data.reasoning: These two cards are one piece of work pretending to be two. Hoisting the support address to a single constant changes what the tests assert against, and relocating those tests moves the same assertions - running them separately means touching the same component and the same test file twice, with the second pass rebasing on the first for no benefit. One worker, separate commits, so each stays revertible. Also folding in the two comments that my own change three commits ago made false: both state that the analytics proxy attaches the page URL to every event and cannot be redacted per event, which stopped being true when the attach became opt-in and scheme-gated. Their conclusions still hold and neither is load-bearing, but leaving them is precisely the failure I spent today documenting on the store-facing docs, and it would be poor form to create a fresh instance of it in the same session. Both files were outside the previous ticket's scope, which is why they were correctly left rather than quietly widened then.

data.decision: Landed lm5aQLBB, and endorsed the worker both exceeding the brief structurally and refusing one instruction in it
data.reasoning: Two judgments worth recording, because both went against what I wrote. First, I asked for the page URL to become opt-in, and the worker observed that a flag is still a convention - which was the original complaint, since the safety held only because one person remembered it. It added a scheme allow-list underneath, so the flag expresses intent while the helper still refuses any URL that is not on an extension page. I verified that: the schemes, the helper, the flag only requesting, and zero call sites opting in. Deliberately an allow-list rather than a deny-list, because a deny-list would need to enumerate every EMR host forever and fails open on the first one missed - the same polarity lesson as the manifest guard earlier today. Second, I suggested a timeout error code and the worker declined it, having traced that the branch producing it is unreachable because no abort signal is ever passed. I confirmed that at the line. Emitting a code that can never occur would put a falsehood in the dashboard rather than a category, so refusing was correct, and a worker that pushes back with evidence is worth more than one that implements every suggestion.

data.decision: Pulled lm5aQLBB; correcting my own claim last pass that no agent-doable work remained
data.reasoning: I told the operator last pass that everything remaining needed them rather than another worker. That was wrong, and worth correcting rather than quietly acting otherwise: four cards I raised myself are agent-doable with no input needed, and I had mentally filed them as follow-ups instead of as work. Of the four this is the one worth doing now. The URL auto-attach at analytics-proxy.ts line 140 puts window.location.href on every captured event unconditionally. It is harmless today because every call site lives in the popup or the options page, so the value resolves to an extension URL - and I confirmed there are zero content-script capture sites, which is not luck but the same restraint recorded in ComplianceDrawer, where instrumentation was refused precisely because that field would carry note identifiers. The problem is the polarity: it fails open. The first content-script capture anyone adds silently ships the EMR note URL, and neither the build nor the tests would notice. That is free to fix now and expensive to discover later, which is the same shape as the allowlist work earlier today. The second half, a raw backend error string forwarded on login failure, is smaller but is the likeliest remaining route for an address to reach analytics.

data.decision: Fixed the third stale reference upstream in intelliforia-shared and re-synced, rather than hand-editing the vendored copy the worker had edited
data.reasoning: The worker did the right thing twice: it made the edit I asked for, and it told me the path was vendored rather than quietly leaving me with a fix that looked correct. I verified both claims - the path is a symlink into .agents/skills, shared.lock.json names the file and its source repo, and the only reads of the store-build variable anywhere are inside the build test's own setup and teardown, so removing it from the release workflow was safe. Landing the vendored edit locally would have been the worse outcome precisely because it would have looked fine: shared:sync would have reverted it later and put the misleading guidance back with nobody watching. Since the upstream repo was cloned locally and clean on main with the pin matching its head, the documented path was open - port the change there, push, and shared:update here. Did that; shared:check now reports no drift. This one mattered beyond tidiness because the stale text tells a developer that console output survives a production build, which after 98854da yields a silent bundle and the conclusion that their tooling is broken - and the whole point of that skill is tracing an extension action to a backend log line.

data.decision: Landed Ttrn0Jm4 as 98854da, accepting that production and staging now emit no console output at all including warnings
data.reasoning: Confirmed the two things the fix turns on before landing: the flag it now uses genuinely covers staging as well as production, at the line that defines it, and the new assertions sit outside the skipped block that surrounds them - otherwise the guarantee would have been written and never executed. The tradeoff I am accepting on the operator's behalf is that production and staging builds now emit nothing at all, warnings and errors included, because the central logger's only sink is the console. I took it because it is not actually new for users - every store build already behaved this way - and because the alternative preserves a path that writes complete clinical notes into a service worker console on a machine we do not control. Losing breadcrumbs for staging testers is a real cost, and there are other diagnostics, so it is a cost rather than a blocker. I also endorse including staging rather than treating it as a developer environment: this repo refreshes staging from a production snapshot, so the data there is production-shaped, and the question that matters for PHI is whose hands the build is in.

data.decision: Pulled Ttrn0Jm4, the last of the four audit code-defects, and filed the two analytics residuals separately rather than folding them in
data.reasoning: This closes the set the documentation audit produced. Confirmed the shape before dispatching: webpack already computes isProduction at line 31 and uses it for mode, devtool and minimize, but drop_console at line 371 and pure_funcs at 373 are gated on STORE_BUILD instead - so the store bundle is clean and every other production build writes full clinical payloads into the service-worker console. The fix is to align that one gate with the isProduction the file already has. Filed the two analytics residuals as their own card rather than folding them into this one. They are both about analytics payloads while this is about console output, and the second of them - the unconditional current-URL attach - is a fails-open structural issue rather than a live leak, so bundling it under a console-logging ticket would have buried it where nobody would look for it later. Keeping this ticket to one concern also keeps its revert clean.

data.decision: Landed Zv1976yZ as two commits and accepted a scope expansion the worker found: the email was also serving as the analytics distinct id
data.reasoning: Confirmed the finding that mattered most before landing, because it was not in the brief and it is worse than what was: auth-store sets the user id to the email whenever the token carries no provider id, and that value was being handed to analytics as the distinct id. The card and my brief both described a leaking property, which exposes an address once per login. A distinct id is sticky and attaches to every subsequent event, so the real exposure was larger than either of us had written down. Accepting a scope expansion is normally the wrong instinct, but here the expansion is the same defect seen properly rather than a different one. I also endorse the worker dropping the EMR instance URL beyond the ask, on the distinction it drew: the product name identifies a product, the instance URL is per-tenant and identifies the customer. The verification I care about is that the gate was proven at the outbound request rather than at an internal flag, and proven twice - once by removing it entirely, and once by removing only the flush-time check, which demonstrated that the three race tests are load-bearing rather than decorative. The split into two commits held its purpose: the urgent removal is revertible without touching the opt-out.

data.decision: Pulled Zv1976yZ ahead of the console-logging defect because the analytics PII is live in the shipped build, and split it into two commits with the PII removal first
data.reasoning: Reordered the two remaining audit defects on exposure rather than on effort. The console-logging one only bites a production build that is not the store build, because drop_console is gated on STORE_BUILD and the release workflow sets it - so the bundle users actually install is clean and the exposure is limited to sideloaded or internal builds. The analytics one fires on every login of every user in the shipped store build right now, sending email and name to a third-party analytics cloud against a policy that promises no PII three times. Live beats latent. Split the card into two commits deliberately. The PII removal is a few lines and needs no design input; the opt-out is a settings surface, a persisted preference and a runtime gate. Bundling them risks the urgent half being held hostage to the larger half, and if the opt-out turns out messier than it looks I still want the PII fix landable on its own. The UX that would normally need deciding is already specified by the document the code is failing: the policy names the location, Settings then Privacy, and the control label, Send Anonymous Usage Data, so the worker is conforming to a written promise rather than inventing an interface.

data.decision: Landed CQgXiLRI as e510666, accepting the in-memory cache over chrome.storage.session on a platform constraint
data.reasoning: Confirmed the one claim the whole fix rests on before landing: a sweep for page-storage writes across the entire extension source returns nothing, and the only surviving reference to the key is a deletion. The worker also proved it against the built bundle rather than the source, which is the honest place to check a leak. Accepted its choice of an in-memory cache over chrome.storage.session because the reasoning is a platform fact rather than a preference - that API defaults to TRUSTED_CONTEXTS, which excludes content scripts, so it would have meant new service-worker wiring to widen an access level on the PHI path, in a ticket scoped to closing a leak. The in-memory route also keeps every signature synchronous, which removes the failure mode I was most worried about when I wrote the brief, namely a caller ignoring a newly returned Promise and silently reading undefined. Worth recording that the fix also removed a latent correctness bug nobody had noticed: the page-storage read was only reachable across page loads, and rehydrating a context that carries its own url and pageTitle handed the caller the previous note's fields under the previous URL.

data.decision: Pulled CQgXiLRI, the page-origin storage leak, as the first of the four code defects the doc audit produced
data.reasoning: Of the four code defects the audit surfaced, this one is both the most clearly wrong and the most contained. A content script writing to sessionStorage writes to the page's origin, not to extension-isolated storage, so a serialized dump of the clinical form the clinician is looking at sits where the EMR's own code, its analytics vendors, and any third-party tag it loads can read it. There is no ambiguity about intent either: the privacy policy already states the correct target state, so this is the code failing to meet a promise rather than a question of what the product should do. Sized it before dispatching - three call sites in one file with two internal callers, and a repo-wide sweep confirms it is the only page-origin storage write in the extension, so the blast radius is one module. Chose it over the analytics card because that one bundles a trivial fix with building an opt-out UI, which carries UX decisions, and over the policy rewrite because that is gated on two questions I cannot answer from the repo. The one real design fork inside this ticket is that chrome.storage.session is asynchronous where sessionStorage is not, so the worker has to establish whether the cache must survive a same-tab navigation before choosing between that and a module-scoped variable.

data.decision: Re-verified the four gravest audit findings against the code myself before propagating them, then split the four code-defects out from the documentation rewrite
data.reasoning: An audit asserting sixteen misrepresentations about PHI handling is exactly the kind of output that does damage if it is wrong, so I checked the four that carry real consequence rather than relaying them. All four hold: note_content is a non-nullable text column on two backend models written on the ordinary scoring and save-gate paths and attributed to provider and organization, against a policy that denies storage three times; the backend contains no OpenRouter code at all while its task map routes note generation to OpenAI and everything else to Gemini, neither of which the policy names; the extension sends email and name on analytics identify against a policy promising no PII; and the options page has four tabs with no Privacy among them against a policy promising an opt-out in its CCPA section. The organising judgment is the split. Four findings are cases where the document is right and the code is wrong - the policy promises something good that the code fails to deliver - and folding those into a documentation rewrite would have quietly converted a set of bugs into a set of edits that make the promises smaller. Those are now separate cards with their own acceptance criteria. I also kept the iOS and extension answers apart deliberately: the app genuinely does not track users, and letting the extension's analytics defect contaminate a true App Store answer would be its own misrepresentation.

data.decision: Raised and pulled a new Priority card to audit every store-facing and legal document against the code, after two were independently found false in one day
data.reasoning: This is me creating work rather than pulling it, which needs justifying. Two separate tickets today each surfaced a document that reaches Apple or Google asserting something the code contradicts - the host-permissions justification claiming the extension never calls OpenRouter directly while background.ts does, and the debugger justification describing a feature with a trigger button that does not exist and daily usage that is actually zero. Neither was found by looking for doc problems; both fell out of unrelated work. All five documents were written on the same day six weeks ago and none has been touched since while the code moved underneath them, so the base rate of staleness is high and the two found are unlikely to be the only two. The stakes are asymmetric: a wrong line in a source file is a bug, but a wrong line in a store justification or a privacy policy is a misrepresentation to a reviewer or a customer on a HIPAA-adjacent product. Scoped it to audit and recommend only, deliberately not to fix, because a false claim can be resolved by correcting the document or by changing the code so the claim becomes true, and choosing between those is a product decision rather than an editing task.

data.decision: Landed the tabs removal as f11c74d and escalated the debugger dead-code discovery to its own Priority card rather than closing it inside a permissions ticket
data.reasoning: Independently confirmed the three claims the whole conclusion rests on, because a permission removal justified by dead code is only as good as the proof that the code is really dead: getRawAccessibilityTree is called at background.ts:2093 and defined nowhere in a class that exposes only captureAXTree and canAttachToTab; CAPTURE_AX_TREE exists solely as its own type and its own switch case with no sender in the codebase; and the chrome:// guard has no callers. All three hold. Accepted the tabs removal on that basis, and recorded rather than hid the shape of the residual risk, which is that Chrome omits url and title instead of raising, so a missed consumer would fail quietly. Did not touch debugger. The card asked for a decision on moving it to optional_permissions, but the finding reframes the question entirely - this is not a used permission that might become optional, it is Chrome's most scrutinised permission being requested from every user at install for a feature that cannot be triggered and would throw if it were. Remove, revive, or defer is a product call, and burying that choice in a permissions audit would have made it invisible. It is now a Priority card of its own with the three options laid out.

data.decision: Pulled OErmV9ZA (#150, permission audit) and scoped the debugger question to analysis-and-recommend rather than change
data.reasoning: Rejected RIrMURiq first: it is a genuine problem but its own card frames the fix as a choice between optional_host_permissions with a per-tenant onboarding prompt and a wildcard that would request access to every Salesforce org on the internet, and its second criterion needs verification against a customer's live org. That is an undecided product decision plus third-party access, which the loop's stop conditions name explicitly, so it is recorded on the card and left. OErmV9ZA is different: two of its three criteria resolve to an audit with a definite answer rather than a preference. Whether anything reads tab.url, tab.title or favIconUrl outside an activeTab grant is a fact about the code, and both outcomes - remove the permission, or demonstrate the paths that need it - are valid deliverables. The tabs permission grants the URL and title of every open tab on a clinician's browser, so removing it if unused is a real privacy reduction on a HIPAA-adjacent product. I scoped the debugger half to analysis and a recommendation only: moving it to optional_permissions changes what a user is prompted for and when, which is a UX decision for the operator, not something to slip into an audit ticket.

data.decision: Landed yf0rkqyS as b8bf1aa on structural verification, and recorded the evidence for narrowing as circumstantial rather than proven
data.reasoning: Verified the two structural claims myself rather than trusting the report, because five reviewer subagents today have failed to deliver a report: there is exactly one isLikelyLocalHost and one validateMatchPatternSchemes in validate-build.js, called from three sites, so the three sections cannot drift apart - which was the main way this fix could rot. And the wiring the worker claimed at three specific line numbers is really there. The judgment worth recording is that I accepted a narrowing justified by absence of counter-evidence rather than by proof. What makes that acceptable is structural rather than documentary: host_permissions has granted only https for these three hosts since ca9192d, so the extension could not have issued a permitted request to a plain-http origin on them, and no breakage was reported in the weeks since. PassageHealth is the weakest of the three because it postdates the Chrome Web Store justification document, and I put that on the card rather than letting a uniform-sounding claim cover an uneven evidence base. The failure mode if I am wrong is visible and recoverable - the extension simply would not activate on that EMR - rather than silent.

All four acceptance criteria verified against the running task rather than asserted:

1. THE LOOP RUNS AND THE INTERVAL IS UNCHANGED. From the hosted logs:
[dispatch] 2026-08-27T16:30:21Z apply=0(ok) sweep=0(ok)
[dispatch] 2026-08-27T16:31:25Z apply=0(ok) sweep=0(ok)
[dispatch] 2026-08-27T16:32:28Z apply=0(ok) sweep=0(ok)
Roughly 63 seconds apart, RELAY_DISPATCH_INTERVAL_SECONDS=60, the same value the compose service passed.

2. NOT-RUNNABLE IS STILL DISTINGUISHABLE. dispatch-loop.sh already prints the word beside the status, so 1 and 127 can never read as the same event. Checked the image actually carries what it needs instead of trusting it - /app/scripts/dispatch-loop.sh present and executable, relay-apply and relay-sweep both on PATH - because shipping this without checking would have produced exactly the silent NOT-RUNNABLE the loop was written to make loud.

3. NO BLAST RADIUS. essential: false. Verified in the running task: relay HEALTHY, cloudflared RUNNING, dispatchers RUNNING as a third container.

4. SEPARATE STREAMS. awslogs-stream-prefix 'dispatch' against /james-brennan/relay, so relay/... and dispatch/... are separable.

Task size raised 512/1024 -> 1024/2048: a third process is small, but a task that OOMs takes the phone line with it.

ONE THING THIS RESOLVED THAT WAS AMBIGUOUS BEFORE. /healthz still reports exceptions_undelivered: 35 and review_links_undelivered: 2, unchanged after the sweep ran. The sweep itself reports '0 review link(s) re-issued (0 still undelivered)'. So those counters are the notify_enabled=false backlog, NOT a missing-sweeper backlog - two causes that were indistinguishable until a sweeper existed to rule one out.

COST OF essential: false, carried forward to JIMB-189: a dead dispatcher now leaves a running task silently. The [dispatch] line every pass is what an absence alarm should watch.

data.body:
RESOLVED in ae1e078, deployed and verified. The mirror was healthy the entire time - the WATCHER was broken.

The sync succeeded on 2026-08-26 at 05:07 UTC: "sync run 01a03c71-5bb9-7404-9e10-b2ded176d19b for 2026-08-26 recorded as succeeded (attempt 1)", generation 15 promoted, 31 created, 152 changed, 183 events. The later "no sync to claim" lines were correct - it was already done.

ROOT CAUSE. watch-nightly.py walked the 96-hour lookback FORWARD from the floor with a hard stop of twenty pages, commented "matches are a handful per lookback". That confuses matches with pages: filter_log_events pages over streams and time, not over hits, so empty pages still consume budget. Six sync-claim streams a night across four nights exhausted twenty pages in the oldest part of the window; the loop stopped early and published the newest match it happened to have seen as though the search had finished. Hence an age that climbed exactly 3600s per hour.

It broke the invariant LOOKBACK_HOURS states about itself - "the cap only bounds the work, never the verdict" - which was true of the lookback and false of the page cap under it.

FIX. Walk backwards from now in slices; the first slice with a match holds the newest one, so work is bounded by how recently the mirror last succeeded rather than by the lookback. An unfinished scan now raises IncompleteScan instead of reporting a partial result, following the rule newest_backup_proof already states: "The failure direction is loud, which is the only acceptable direction for a watcher."

VERIFIED, against live CloudWatch rather than stubs:
before newest proof 2026-08-25T05:07:56 age 45.57h BREACH
after newest proof 2026-08-26T05:07:59 age 22.00h HEALTHY

Published metric flipped at 23:09 EDT: 45.82h -> 22.02h. The alarm needs four consecutive healthy datapoints at 15-minute intervals, so it self-clears about an hour later.

TWO THINGS WORTH KEEPING FROM THIS. The existing tests passed throughout, because the only multi-page case they exercised was two pages - the new tests assert the shape rather than the count. And the alarm did its job: JIMB-153 built it and it fired. What failed after that was the response - nineteen hours passed with one email subscriber and nobody acting. A detector nobody reads is not detection, and that half is still open.

BLOCKED BY JIMB-163, and this is not a sequencing preference.

Nothing in production applies an approval. relay-apply runs nowhere: the ECS task's containers are ['relay','cloudflared'], relay.json has no command override so the image CMD is uvicorn alone, app.py starts no consumer in-process, and no EventBridge rule invokes it.

So a toggle shipped today would take Jim's tap, mint a durable command, answer 200, and the note would never land. That is worse than no toggle - it converts "nothing happened" into "Jim believes it happened".

The write channel itself is BUILT and deliberately inert (commits a4eab35, 38466ff, cb3d73d): POST /surface/approve/{token} on the relay, api/approve.ts on the Worker, the Clerk-email to relay-approver map, and GET /surface/closeout/{token}/write handing the card the exact note bytes and digest. RELAY_SURFACE_WRITE_TOKEN is unset on both sides, so the Worker answers 503 and the relay 404s.

Order: JIMB-163, then prove the write (JIMB-191), then provision the token, then the toggle.

VERIFIED 2026-08-27 — the relay cutover happened and this did not come with it. Nothing applies approvals or sweeps in production.

Evidence:
- aws ecs describe-task-definition james-brennan-relay:2 -> containers are ['relay','cloudflared']. There is no dispatcher container.
- relay.json has no `command` override, so the task runs the image CMD: uvicorn relay.app:app. Web server only.
- src/relay/app.py has no lifespan, no on_event startup, no create_task and no EffectConsumer reference, so nothing runs in-process either.
- aws scheduler list-schedules / aws events list-rules -> no schedule or rule invokes relay-apply or relay-sweep anywhere.

Two consequences, and the second is the quiet one:

1. relay-apply. Approvals mint a durable command that nothing will ever deliver. /healthz reports effect_commands_undelivered: 0 today ONLY because nothing has been approved in production yet. The defect is latent and it arms on the first real approval — which is the moment the pilot goes live.

2. relay-sweep. This is the half that "notices the things that fail by not happening — a run that stopped mid-call, a review link whose send was interrupted, a package past its due time." It is not running, so that whole class of failure is currently invisible.

This now blocks JIMB-182 (approve from the card). A switch that mints a command nothing applies would report success to Jim while the note never lands.

VERIFIED LIVE 2026-08-27 — this shipped unmitigated and is armed in production right now.

aws ecs describe-task-definition --task-definition james-brennan-relay:2
volumes : NONE
relay mountPoints=none
cloudflared mountPoints=none

Neither escape route was taken. There is no EFS mount, and the spool is still a filesystem path (config.py:352 spool_dir, :411 spool_path) — no migration under migrations/versions/ mentions a spool table, so it did not fold into PostgreSQL with JIMB-89 either.

So the exact sentence in this ticket is now a description of production: the relay runs on Fargate with an ephemeral task filesystem, and a deploy, a scale event or a task replacement destroys /data/spool/voice-closeout/. The continuity runbook calls those files "a call a technician actually made whose store write failed. It may be the only copy in the world."

/healthz reports spooled_closeouts: 0, so nothing is at risk this minute. That is luck, not mitigation — and it means the fix can land with no data to migrate, which will not be true later.

Raised from "this week" to URGENT and moved out of Backlog. The recommendation in the ticket body still stands: fold the spool into PostgreSQL rather than hosting a filesystem the relay must not lose.

ticket.description_html:
Extend the pj board command with five read-only subcommands that resolve the project implicitly by walking up from CWD to the nearest .project.json.

AC:

  • board provider prints plane|trello|linear
  • board slug prints the project slug string
  • board status prints tickets in 'started' state groups, most recently added/updated first
  • board recent [n] prints the n (default 5) most recently added/updated tickets from any state

ticket.description_html:
THE WORST THING IN THE SYSTEM RIGHT NOW. Verified 2026-08-27 by direct probe of Twilio, the workstation and AWS.

The phone line and the closeout store are in different places and neither knows it.

- Twilio IncomingPhoneNumbers: +18668904137 VoiceUrl = https://voice.ipm.automaticai.io/twilio/stream [POST]. That is the PRIMARY answerer and it is the `voice` container on big-chungus. The AWS relay is only the VoiceFallbackUrl.
- That voice container writes store_backend=sqlite at /data/relay.db, in docker volume relay_relay-data on the workstation. It currently holds 45 closeouts, 61 versions, 22 transcript turns, 37 notifications.
- The production relay reads PostgreSQL brennan-relay-pg in AWS. It never reads that SQLite file. The ECS dispatchers never sweep it.

So: Frank makes a call -> the closeout is captured -> it lands in a file on a personal laptop -> Jim's surface never shows it, no review link is sent, no dispatcher applies it, and every health check stays green.

Nothing has been lost YET only because there have been no calls since 2026-08-26T00:32:06Z (relay.db mtime). The wiring is live and the next real call exercises it.

MADE WORSE BY TWO BROKEN EDGES, both silent:
- voice -> local relay forward: RELAY_LIVE_FORWARD_URL=http://relay:18090/surface/live. The local relay is stopped and off the network. `docker exec voice python -c "socket.gethostbyname('relay')"` -> gaierror [Errno -2]. The forward is fire-and-forget with failures swallowed.
- voice -> AWS relay: `urlopen('https://relay.ipm.automaticai.io/healthz')` from inside the container -> HTTP 403 Forbidden. So even if it were repointed it could not currently reach production.

This is the true content of JIMB-185. Migrating voice is not a tidiness exercise about where a container runs - it is the fix for a data path that currently drops the client's work on the floor.

Ordering note: do NOT flip RELAY_EGRESS_ENABLED (JIMB-191) before this is resolved. Egress on top of a split store means the half of the closeouts that live in AWS get written to GorillaDesk and the half on the laptop never do, with no way to tell which is which afterwards.

So the pilot's core loop — Frank calls, a closeout is captured, Jim approves, a note lands on the customer record — has not run end to end in production even once.

3. Blocked by JIMB-163 regardless — with no dispatcher deployed, an approval mints a command nothing applies, so flipping the gates first would produce approvals that look accepted and never land.

Related: JIMB-125 (approval is a passcode, not the decided passkey — "egress stays off until"), JIMB-94 (forced-failure rehearsal and release evidence packet).

THE CLIENT'S PHONE NUMBER TERMINATES ON A PERSONAL WORKSTATION. +18668904137 -> Twilio Media Streams -> wss://voice.ipm.automaticai.io/ws-twilio -> the `voice` container on big-chungus, via the local cloudflare tunnel.

Verified 2026-08-26: there is NO ECS task-definition family for voice (only james-brennan-relay, james-brennan-relay-publish, and the five mirror families), NO ECR repository, and no reference to apps/voice anywhere under devops/. The relay cutover moved apps/relay and left this behind.

Consequences today: if the workstation sleeps, reboots, loses power, or its tunnel restarts, Frank calls a number that does not answer. There is no alarm on it and no second instance.

WHAT IT NEEDS (it is not a lift-and-shift):
- an ECR repo james-brennan/voice and an ECS service in cluster james-brennan-relay, with a cloudflared sidecar, matching the relay's shape
- a LONG-LIVED WEBSOCKET, which is the hard part. Twilio Media Streams holds the socket open for the whole call. Fargate deployment draining and the tunnel's idle behaviour both need checking against a live call, not assumed.
- secrets into SSM as SecureStrings: Deepgram, Cartesia, the LLM key, Twilio. Same pattern as the relay's /james-brennan/relay/prod/* set.
- the voice service also talks to the relay; RELAY_* URLs must point at relay.ipm.automaticai.io, not a local address.
- the tunnel ingress for voice.ipm.automaticai.io moves from ~/docker/core/cloudflare-tunnel-automaticai/config.yml to the sidecar. Both claiming it is the same race that just bit the relay.

Owner has stated the requirement plainly: no client infrastructure on his personal server except a dev stack he explicitly brings up.

ticket.description_html:
Extend the pj board command with five read-only subcommands that resolve the project implicitly by walking up from CWD to the nearest .project.json.

AC:

  • board provider prints plane|trello|linear
  • board slug prints the project slug string
  • board status prints tickets in 'started' state groups, most recently added/updated first
  • board recent [n] prints the n (default 5) most recently added/updated tickets from any state
  • board modules prints the project's modules

All support --json. Plane v1 ignores state/state_group query filters, so started-state selection must be client-side against the project's states map.

ticket.description_html:
relay-dispatchers runs relay-apply and relay-sweep on a 60-second loop. The mirror's hosted pattern — EventBridge Scheduler launching a Fargate task — cannot serve that: a Fargate cold start is measured in tens of seconds, so a per-minute schedule would spend most of its life starting up, and would bill for it.

So the dispatchers belong in the same task definition as the relay, as a second container. That also preserves the property the continuity runbook depends on: the web process has no timer at all. Everything that happens without somebody pressing something happens in the dispatcher container, and keeping the two co-located keeps that sentence true.

Acceptance criteria

  1. The dispatch loop runs in the hosted task and its interval is unchanged.
  2. NOT-RUNNABLE is still distinguishable from a red exit in the hosted logs — sweep=1 and sweep=127 mean opposite things and the log line must still say which.
  3. A red dispatcher exit does not restart or replace the web container.
  4. CloudWatch shows the two containers' streams separately.

ticket.description_html:
LIVE INCIDENT as of 2026-08-27 02:50 UTC. This is not a design gap; it is happening now.

aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names james-brennan-mirror-sync-absent
state : ALARM
since : 2026-08-26T07:58:33-04:00 (~19 hours in alarm)
reason : NightlyProofAgeSeconds crossed 108000 (30h)

Current metric value, JamesBrennan/Mirror NightlyProofAgeSeconds, Tenant=brennan/prod Kind=sync:
2026-08-26T21:50 EDT -> 164045 seconds = 45.6 HOURS, and still climbing 3600/hour.

The watcher is healthy — it is publishing hourly. It is the SYNC that has not proved itself.

Why it matters, from the alarm's own description: "A missed sync breaks the JIMB-149 parity property." JIMB-149 is Done and its whole claim is that the daily sync boundary is what makes the shadow system provable. That claim is currently false.

Detection worked. JIMB-153 built exactly this alarm and it fired correctly. What did not work is the response: the SNS topic james-brennan-mirror-alerts has one subscriber, jaradd@gmail.com by email, and 19 hours passed with nobody acting. Worth establishing whether that email arrived, went to spam, or is simply not a channel anybody watches — a detector nobody reads is not detection.

Note the sibling alarm james-brennan-mirror-backup-absent is OK, so backups are still proving themselves. Only sync is failing.

ticket.description_html:
The Cockpit (/cockpit) reads inventory:v1 from KV. The ONLY thing that writes that key is james-brennan-surface-inventory.timer, a --user systemd timer on the workstation, running nightly.

Verified 2026-08-26: EventBridge Scheduler holds james-brennan-surface-publish (bundle:v1) plus four mirror schedules. There is NO schedule for inventory. Live inventory:v1 at time of writing was 8 hours old.

So the bundle publisher made it to the cloud in the cutover and this one did not. If the workstation is off, the Cockpit freezes at the last good inventory and /api/health stays green — the exact failure mode AGENTS.md already documents for the bundle publisher: "a stale surface looks like a healthy one".

THE FIX IS SMALL AND THE PATTERN ALREADY EXISTS. james-brennan-surface-publish is an EventBridge schedule firing a one-shot ECS task from the james-brennan-relay-publish family. This needs the same thing. The wrinkle: the inventory publisher reads the mirror, which is in-VPC only (brennan-mirror-pg is PubliclyAccessible=false), so the task must run in the VPC with the mirror's security group — which is exactly what scripts/mirror-surface-publish-vpc.sh already does by hand.

Do this at the same time as JIMB-182's dispatcher work if convenient; both are "a scheduled ECS task that nobody has written the taskdef for yet".

ticket.description_html:
The hosting half of JIMB-156. JIMB-140 is the precedent — it moved the mirror's compute off this same workstation onto Fargate + EventBridge. The difference is shape, not principle: the mirror's workers are batch, the relay is a long-running service holding WebSockets (wss://.../cr) and an SSE channel (GET /surface/live).

Blocked by JIMB-89. RELAY_STORE_BACKEND=sqlite is what pins the relay to a Docker volume on a personal disk. The cutover is what unpins it, and it is already written and rehearsable. Target a second database on the existing brennan-mirror-pg — $0 of additional instance cost.

Ingress is a decision, recorded here rather than assumed:

  • ALB (recommended) — roughly $18/month, WebSockets and SSE both supported, and every hop in the call path lives in the client's own account. That last property is the whole point of the ticket.
  • cloudflared sidecar — $0, keeps the current hostname, but puts Cloudflare in the critical path of a phone line and adds a moving part to the thing being made simpler.

Fargate ARM64, public subnet with assignPublicIp, egress through the existing IGW — the same no-NAT reasoning as devops/ecs/README.md. Secrets resolve from SSM SecureStrings, not from a file. Expect the account's bill to move from about $22/month to about $55.

Acceptance criteria

  1. The relay answers on infrastructure in 067200612963 and on no personal machine.
  2. A real inbound call completes end to end against the hosted endpoint, and the completed closeout is visible in the store.
  3. The WebSocket leg and the Engine Room's SSE channel both survive the ingress choice — proven by a call and by a live room, not by documentation.
  4. The image is an immutable tag in ECR, built by a task, not by docker compose on somebody's laptop.
  5. The chosen ingress option, and the reason the other was rejected, is written into devops/ecs/README.md.
  6. The local path stays runnable and is disabled only after criterion 2 passes.

cloudflared sidecar — $0, keeps the current hostname, but puts Cloudflare in the
critical path of a phone line and adds a moving part to the thing being made simpler.

Fargate ARM64, public subnet with assignPublicIp, egress through the existing
IGW — the same no-NAT reasoning as devops/ecs/README.md. Secrets resolve from SSM
SecureStrings, not from a file. Expect the account's bill to move from about $22/month to
about $55.
Acceptance criteria

The relay answers on infrastructure in 067200612963 and on no personal machine.
A real inbound call completes end to end against the hosted endpoint, and the completed
closeout is visible in the store.
The WebSocket leg and the Engine Room's SSE channel both survive the ingress choice —
proven by a call and by a live room, not by documentation.
The image is an immutable tag in ECR, built by a task, not by docker compose
on somebody's laptop.
The chosen ingress option, and the reason the other was rejected, is written into
devops/ecs/README.md.
The local path stays runnable and is disabled only after criterion 2 passes.

ticket.description_html:
relay-dispatchers runs relay-apply and relay-sweep on a 60-second loop. The mirror's hosted pattern — EventBridge Scheduler launching a Fargate task — cannot serve that: a Fargate cold start is measured in tens of seconds, so a per-minute schedule would spend most of its life starting up, and would bill for it.

So the dispatchers belong in the same task definition as the relay, as a second container. That also preserves the property the continuity runbook depends on: the web process has no timer at all. Everything that happens without somebody pressing something happens in the dispatcher container, and keeping the two co-located keeps that sentence true.

Acceptance criteria

  1. The dispatch loop runs in the hosted task and its interval is unchanged.
  2. NOT-RUNNABLE is still distinguishable from a red exit in the hosted logs — sweep=1 and sweep=127 mean opposite things and the log line must still say which.
  3. A red dispatcher exit does not restart or replace the web container.
  4. CloudWatch shows the two containers' streams separately.

ticket.description_html:
The relay's own continuity runbook says it plainly, in the three lines it asks an operator to read before anything else:

Never delete a spool file. A file under /data/spool/voice-closeout/ is a call a technician actually made whose store write failed. It may be the only copy in the world.

On the current host that path is a Docker volume, which persists. On Fargate the task filesystem is ephemeral — a deploy, a scale event, or a task replacement destroys it. Moving the relay to Fargate without resolving this converts a documented recovery path into silent data loss, and the loss is exactly the calls that already failed once.

Two ways out: an EFS mount, or fold the spool into PostgreSQL as part of JIMB-89 so the failed-write queue is a table rather than a directory. The second is better — it removes the concept of a filesystem the relay must not lose, rather than hosting one.

Acceptance criteria

  1. A spooled closeout survives a deliberate task replacement, proven by replacing the task while one is spooled.
  2. Whichever mechanism is chosen, continuity-runbook.md is updated — the recovery instructions currently name a filesystem path.
  3. The spool's depth is visible from outside the box, so a growing queue is a signal and not a discovery.

AC

  • n8n webhook as Plane Bloodbank event provenance

  • Events normalized to 33GOD pjangler/krebs/lifecycle standard (we will define now)

    • Pjangler event (planned)`project.board.created`returns a slug

    • Plane emits plane.board.created, plane.ticket.transitioned, etc

    • Envelopes contain board_id,slug,workspace,etc.

    • Payloads contain associated json serialized entity i.e. ticket, board

  • These new events added to Bloodbank n8n node package so I can start creating event-driven workflows that bind to plane actions. i.e. I add Bloodbank node "On Ticket Created" (binds toplane.ticket.created)
